h1: Festbier or Marzen? What Oktoberfest really pours today
title: Festbier or Märzen at Oktoberfest? | Craft Beer School
desc: Festbier and Märzen compared: why Oktoberfest now pours golden festbier, how the two styles differ and what amber Märzen still offers.
teaser: Picture an Oktoberfest beer and you probably see amber. At the Munich Wiesn today, the beer in your stein is golden.
standfirst: Märzen is the beer most people associate with Oktoberfest. Yet the beer poured in Munich's tents today is a paler, lighter festbier. Here is how that happened and how the two styles differ in the glass.
sections:
Oktoberfest began in 1810 as a celebration of a royal wedding in Munich and grew into the world's best known beer festival. Only Munich breweries that meet the festival's rules may pour in the main tents. Today that means six: Augustiner, Hacker Pschorr, Hofbräu, Löwenbräu, Paulaner and Spaten.

For much of the 19th and 20th centuries, the festival beer was an amber lager in the Märzen tradition. Our guide to Märzen and Oktoberfest covers that history in depth.

Märzen means March beer. Before refrigeration, Bavarian brewing was restricted in summer because warm weather made spoilage likely. Brewers made a stronger beer in March, stored it in cool cellars through the summer and drank the last of it in autumn. Long cold storage, or lagering, made it smooth and clean.

Modern Märzen is amber to copper, around 5.8 to 6.3% ABV in BJCP terms. It is built on Munich and Vienna malts, which give rich bread crust and toasted flavours. Hop bitterness is moderate and the finish fairly dry. Our Vienna lager guide covers its close cousin.

Festbier is the beer poured at Oktoberfest today. It is golden, roughly 5.8 to 6.3% ABV in BJCP terms, so similar in strength to Märzen. The difference is colour and malt. Festbier uses mostly pilsner malt with some Vienna or Munich, giving a lighter, bready, slightly sweet flavour instead of rich toast.

It drinks easily for its strength. That is partly the point: Oktoberfest beer is served by the litre in a mass stein. A lighter body suits a long day in a crowded tent. Festbier sits closer to a strong helles than to a classic Märzen.

Through the second half of the 20th century, Munich breweries moved their Wiesn beers paler, in step with drinkers' growing preference for golden lager. By the 1990s, most of the tent beers were golden. Some breweries still make a traditional amber Märzen for export or for their own taprooms, but in Munich the festival style is now festbier.

Outside Germany, many breweries still label an amber Märzen as "Oktoberfest". That is why American and Indian taprooms often pour amber beers in autumn while Munich pours gold. Neither is wrong. They are two related styles with a shared history.

Pour both at around 6 to 8 °C in similar glasses. Look at the colour first: golden versus amber or copper. Smell the festbier for fresh bread, light honey and a hint of floral hops. Smell the Märzen for toasted bread crust and light caramel.

On the palate, the festbier feels lighter and softer, finishing clean. The Märzen feels fuller, with more toast and a dry, malty finish. Bitterness is moderate in both. Taste one, rinse with water, taste the other, then switch back.

The differences are clearer in a good fresh example. Imported versions that sat warm for weeks may taste of honey or cardboard instead. Learning to separate staling from malt character takes practice.

The two styles differ mainly in the grist. A Märzen leans on Munich and Vienna malts, sometimes with a small amount of light caramel malt, which gives colour and toasty depth. A festbier is mostly pilsner malt with a smaller share of Vienna or Munich, so it stays golden and tastes lighter.

Both are fermented cool with lager yeast, roughly 8 to 12 °C, then lagered cold for several weeks so the flavour settles and the beer clears. Traditional German breweries may use decoction mashing for both, which adds malt depth without needing caramel malt.

Both beers suit Bavarian festival food: roast chicken, pork knuckle, pretzels, sausages and potato dishes. In India they work well with tandoori chicken, seekh kebabs, chole bhature and grilled paneer. Märzen's toastier malt suits darker, roasted flavours. Festbier is better with lighter, fried or salty food.

A one litre stein of 6% beer contains a lot of alcohol. If you try a festival style at a brewpub, order a half litre or smaller, eat well and pace yourself with water.

The Märzen and festbier story shows how beer styles change with drinkers, brewing technology and even festival logistics. A style is a snapshot, not a fixed rule. Brewers who understand those shifts can make deliberate choices instead of copying labels. That kind of grounding in history, ingredients and process is what style study is for.
faqs: What beer is served at Oktoberfest today?
Mostly festbier: a golden, strong lager around 6% ABV from the six Munich breweries allowed to pour there.
Is Märzen the same as Oktoberfest beer?
Historically, yes. Many breweries outside Munich still call their amber Märzen an Oktoberfest beer, but the Munich tents now pour golden festbier.
Which is stronger, festbier or Märzen?
They are similar, both roughly 5.8 to 6.3% ABV. The main differences are colour and malt character.
